how-much-does-a-vending-machine-actually.text:
← Vending machine route margin calculator

How much does a vending machine actually make?

Route listings and machine sellers quote sales. Sales are the easiest number to produce and the least useful one to own. Here is the same machine described in gross revenue and in what actually reaches you.

Open the free route margin calculator

$294.00 a month in sales, $63.71 in profit

A snack machine sells 42 units per restock at $1.75, with $0.55 of product cost per unit, on a 15% commission split with the location. You visit four times a month: 12 minutes restocking, 20 minutes of round-trip drive, 8 miles. Your own time is worth $22 an hour, cashless sales cost 2.6%, shrink runs 3%, and the machine amortizes at $15 a month.

Per visitAmount
Gross revenue (42 × $1.75)$73.50
Cost of goods, including 3% shrink$23.79
Location commission (15% of gross)$11.03
Card processing (2.6%)$1.91
Your labor (32 min at $22/hr)$11.73
Mileage (8 × $0.67)$5.36
Machine cost, amortized$3.75
Total cost$57.57
Net profit per visit$15.93
Margin21.7%
Monthly profit (4 visits)$63.71

The machine turns over $294.00 a month and hands you $63.71. Notice what the second-largest deduction is, after the product itself: not the commission, not the card fees — your own time, at $11.73 a visit. Most back-of-envelope vending maths prices that at zero, which is exactly what makes a marginal location look like a good one.

Drive time decides a location, not sales

Hold the sales completely constant — same 42 units, same price, same commission — and move only how far away the machine is:

Round-trip driveLaborMileageProfit / visitProfit / monthEffective hourly
5 minutes (2 miles)$6.23$1.34$25.45$101.79$89.82
20 minutes (8 miles)$11.73$5.36$15.93$63.71$29.86
35 minutes (15 miles)$17.23$10.05$5.74$22.95$7.32

Same machine, same sales, and the third row is a job that pays $7.32 an hour. A busy location an hour away is routinely worth less than a quiet one on a loop you already drive. This is the first thing to evaluate about a placement offer and the last thing the pitch mentions, because the owner making the offer does not bear the drive.

The commission split costs more than its percentage

Commission comes off gross revenue, before any of your costs. So it is a slice of the whole pie taken out of a margin that was only ever a sliver of it:

Location commissionProfit / visitProfit / month
0%$26.95$107.81
15%$15.93$63.71
25%$8.58$34.31

Moving from 15% to 25% costs the location 10 points of their revenue share and costs you 46% of your remaining profit. That asymmetry is worth naming out loud in a negotiation: a split that sounds like a small concession on their side is often most of the margin on yours.

How many machines is a living?

Three locations of the quality above produce $191.13 a month. Reaching $3,000 a month means adding 45 more, for 48 in total.

FigureValue
Locations3
Average profit per location$63.71
Total monthly profit$191.13
Target monthly income$3,000.00
Gap$2,808.87
Additional locations needed45

That number is not a verdict on the business — it is a verdict on locations of this quality, and it moves fast. Better commission terms, higher-volume placements, or a tighter route each cut it substantially; worse terms push it past what one person can physically service. The point of computing it is that "how many machines do I need?" has an answer, and it is worth having before buying the first one rather than after the tenth.

Where the "passive income" pitch breaks down

Look again at where the money goes: on a 20-minute drive, one visit is about 32 minutes of committed time returning $15.93, or $29.86 an hour. That is a fair rate for skilled self-employed work — and it is a wage, not a passive return. The 35-minute row earns $7.32 an hour for the same work. The business is real. Any pitch that leaves the operator's hours out of the arithmetic has left out the largest line.

Common questions

How much does one vending machine actually make per month?

Far less than its sales suggest. A machine selling 42 units a visit at 1.75 dollars, restocked four times a month, grosses 294 dollars a month. After cost of goods, a 15 percent location commission, card processing fees, shrink, mileage, your own restock and drive time, and the machine's amortized cost, it nets 63.71 dollars a month. That is a 21.7 percent margin, and the single largest deduction is not the product, it is your time getting there and back.

Why does drive time matter more than sales volume for a vending location?

Because the drive is a fixed cost per visit that sales volume does not reduce. The same machine, selling exactly the same 42 units, nets 101.79 dollars a month on a 5-minute drive, 63.71 dollars on a 20-minute drive, and 22.95 dollars on a 35-minute drive. Nothing about the location's sales changed across those three figures. A busy machine an hour away can easily be worth less than a quiet one on your existing loop, which is why route density is the first thing to evaluate about an offer and the last thing an owner's pitch mentions.

How many vending machines do I need for a full-time income?

More than most route pitches imply. At 63.71 dollars of monthly profit per location, three machines produce 191.13 dollars a month. Reaching 3,000 dollars a month from locations of that quality means adding 45 more, for 48 in total. That number moves fast with location quality: better commission terms, higher volume, or a tighter route can cut it substantially, and worse terms can push it beyond what one operator can physically service. Running your own numbers before buying a machine is the difference between a route business and an expensive hobby.

How much does the location commission split cost me?

It comes off gross revenue before any of your costs, so it bites harder than its percentage suggests. On the same machine, no commission leaves 107.81 dollars of monthly profit, a 15 percent split leaves 63.71 dollars, and a 25 percent split leaves 34.31 dollars. Going from 15 to 25 percent removes nearly half the remaining profit, because the commission is a share of revenue while what you keep is a much smaller share of the same revenue. A location asking for a higher split is asking for a far larger fraction of your margin than of their own sales.

What costs do new vending operators leave out?

Their own labor, first and most expensive. Restocking and driving are work, and pricing them at zero is what makes a losing location look profitable. After that: card processing fees, which are a percentage of every cashless sale; shrink and spoilage from theft, jams, and expiry; mileage as a real vehicle cost rather than just fuel; and the machine's own amortized cost, since a machine bought once still has to earn back its replacement. Leaving any of these out inflates the profit on every location equally, so the ranking between locations stays plausible while every number in it is wrong.

Is a vending route passive income?

Not in the sense the phrase is usually sold. The arithmetic here is dominated by the operator's own time: on a 20-minute drive, restocking one location is about 32 minutes of committed time for 15.93 dollars of profit, an effective 29.86 dollars an hour. That is a reasonable rate for skilled self-employed work, and it is a wage rather than a passive return. On a 35-minute drive the same visit works out to 7.32 dollars an hour. The business is real; the passivity is not, and any route pitch that omits the operator's hours is omitting the largest line.

Run it on a location you are considering

The calculator takes your own units, prices, commission split, drive time and labor rate, reports profit per visit and per month with the effective hourly rate, rolls a list of locations into route profit, and says how many more a target income needs. It runs entirely in your browser.

Common questions

Why does shrink (theft or spoilage) add extra cost instead of just lowering my sales count?

Because you already paid for those units when you loaded the machine — they were product cost, not lost revenue. Treating shrink as a hit to sales undercounts how much theft or spoiled stock is actually costing you; this calculator adds it on top of the cost of the units you did sell, so the real product cost shows up.

Why does commission come out of gross sales rather than my profit?

Because that is how nearly every vending placement agreement is written — the location owner is paid a percentage of what the machine takes in, not a share of what is left after your costs. Commission is one of the first numbers charged to a visit here, before card fees, mileage, or your own labor.

Why allocate the machine's monthly cost across each visit instead of tracking it separately?

A machine you are still paying off or leasing costs money whether or not a location sells well. Spreading that fixed cost across the visits you actually make each month is what turns "this location has $73 in sales" into "this location is worth keeping," the number that actually decides whether to renegotiate commission or pull the machine.

Does anything about my locations or sales get uploaded?

No. Every field on this page runs in your browser only. Nothing is sent to a server, there is no account, and the location list you type into the route section is never saved anywhere — it exists only in the page while it is open. The visit inputs above and the target monthly income setting are different: those are saved locally on this device, so you don't retype them, and a shareable link can carry them to another device. Usage counting only tallies anonymous feature events, and you can turn it off with the button above.

vs-cantaloupe.html.text:

This calculator vs. Cantaloupe Seed

Cantaloupe's Seed products are a full vending management platform built around its own cashless card-reader hardware: real-time telemetry from every machine, remote price changes, inventory and depletion alerts, restock predictions, and route-scheduling tools across a whole fleet. Per Cantaloupe's own published pricing page, base subscription plans start around $18.95/month, with operators typically budgeting roughly $8-12 per machine per month in telemetry and software fees on top of the hardware itself. Seed Cashless+ and Seed Pro are paid software tiers quoted per fleet on top of that. This calculator charges nothing, needs no hardware, and reads no machine directly -- it is a static page you type numbers into.

That makes Cantaloupe's Seed the right tool for running cashless payments and telemetry across a fleet of machines. This calculator answers a narrower question, for an operator who already has sales and cost figures for a location (from a DEX report, a cashless dashboard, or a manual count): is this specific location actually profitable, and does the whole route add up to my income goal?

QuestionWhere to answer it
Take cashless payments and get real-time sales telemetry from a machine? Cantaloupe's cashless readers and Seed software, or a similar VMS.
Get alerted when a slot is running low, or auto-generate restock pick lists? Seed Cashless+ / Seed Pro's inventory and restock-prediction tools.
How much does Cantaloupe's own software and telemetry cost per machine? Cantaloupe's published pricing page -- this calculator charges no subscription or per-machine fee of its own.
Is this one location actually profitable once commission, card fees, shrink, drive time, and machine cost are counted? This calculator's per-visit profit.
Does my whole list of locations add up to my monthly income goal? This calculator's route rollup.

Common questions

Should I use this calculator or Cantaloupe Seed?

They solve different problems at different scales. Cantaloupe's Seed products (Seed Cashless+ and Seed Pro) are a vending management platform: cashless card readers with built-in telemetry, remote price changes, inventory and restock-prediction alerts, and route-scheduling tools, sold as an ongoing software subscription on top of hardware you buy or lease. This calculator has no hardware, no telemetry, and no account at all -- it is a free one-page arithmetic check for whether a single location's numbers, that you type in yourself, actually add up to a profit once commission, card fees, shrink, drive time, and the machine's own cost are counted.

How much does Cantaloupe's software cost?

Per Cantaloupe's own published pricing page for Cantaloupe One, base subscription plans start around $18.95/month, and operators should plan for roughly $8-12 per machine per month in telemetry and software fees on top of that, plus the cashless reader hardware itself. Seed Cashless+ is described as a paid software subscription layered on top; Cantaloupe does not publish a flat price for it or for Seed Pro, both of which are quoted per fleet. This calculator has no subscription, no hardware requirement, and no per-machine fee -- it is a free static page.

Does this replace Cantaloupe's telemetry or cashless payment hardware?

No, and it is not trying to. This tool cannot read a machine's actual sales, cannot take a cashless payment, and cannot alert you when a slot is empty -- all of that requires the sensors and card readers Cantaloupe's hardware provides. This calculator only takes the numbers you already have (from a DEX report, a cashless dashboard, or your own count) and turns them into a profit-per-visit and a monthly route rollup. Plenty of operators running Cantaloupe or a competing telemetry platform still do this specific gut-check by hand or in a spreadsheet; this replaces the spreadsheet, not the telemetry.

vs-judging-a-location-by-gross-sales-alo.text:

This calculator vs. judging a location by gross sales alone

A location report that reads "$105.00 in sales this visit" looks like the better stop next to one that reads "$66.50" -- until commission, card fees, shrink, drive time, and the machine's own monthly cost come out. Gross sales is revenue before every one of those costs, and none of them is the same percentage of sales at every location: a location farther from home base, or on a steeper commission split, or with more shrink, can look bigger on the sales line and still be the worse stop once its own costs are counted against it.

That makes gross sales the right number for knowing what a machine took in. It cannot answer the question that decides whether to keep, renegotiate, or drop a location: what did this visit actually net, after everything it cost to run?

QuestionWhere to answer it
What did the machine take in since the last visit? Gross sales -- a DEX report, a cashless dashboard, or your own count.
What did commission, card fees, and shrink actually take out of that? This calculator's per-visit breakdown.
Was the drive worth your own time at the rate you want to earn? This calculator's mileage and labor lines, folded into the same result.
Is this specific location actually profitable once the machine's own cost is counted? This calculator's net profit per visit.
Does my whole route add up to my monthly income goal? This calculator's route rollup.
Price your own location and route

Two locations, one gross-sales ranking that flips

Run through this calculator's own arithmetic, same restock frequency for both: Location A sells 60 units at $1.75 with a 25% commission, a 5% shrink rate, and a 35-minute round-trip drive, for $105.00 in gross sales. Location B sells 38 units at the same price with a 10% commission, 2% shrink, and an 8-minute round trip, for $66.50 -- 37% less than A on the sales line alone.

Once commission, card fees, shrink, mileage, restock labor at $22/hr, and the machine's own monthly cost are taken out, A's costs come to $96.67 against B's $42.06. A nets $8.33 for the visit (about $33.31 projected for the month at 4 visits); B nets $24.44 for the visit (about $97.77 projected for the month) -- B, the location with 37% less gross sales, nets nearly three times A's monthly profit. A gross-sales ranking would have kept A and questioned B; the actual costs say the opposite.

Not a claim about your own locations -- both are illustrative inputs to this calculator's own published arithmetic, chosen to show how commission, shrink, and drive time can outweigh a sales-line difference. Your own numbers may rank the other way, or not flip at all; that is exactly what typing them into the fields above tells you and a sales report alone cannot.

This tool needs no account, no DEX file, and no telemetry: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and the numbers you type in stay on your device -- nothing is uploaded anywhere.

Common questions

Why is gross sales a bad way to rank vending locations?

Because gross sales is revenue before commission, card fees, shrink, mileage, your own restock labor, and the machine's own cost are taken out -- and those five costs are not the same percentage of sales at every location. A location with a 25% commission split and a 35-minute round trip can post higher gross sales than a location with a 10% split five minutes away, and still net far less profit, because the costs that gross sales ignores are larger there.

How big is the gap in practice?

Using this calculator's own arithmetic on two illustrative locations at the same restock frequency: Location A sells 60 units at $1.75 with a 25% commission, 5% shrink, and a 35-minute round trip, for $105.00 in gross sales -- 58% more than Location B's $66.50. But A's costs (commission, card fee, shrink, mileage, labor, machine share) come to $96.67 against B's $42.06, so A nets $8.33 a visit ($33.31 projected for the month) while B nets $24.44 a visit ($97.77 projected for the month) -- B, the location with the lower gross sales, makes nearly three times the monthly profit.

Does a higher commission or longer drive always mean lower profit?

Not always -- a location can have a high commission or a long drive and still be the better stop if its sales volume is high enough to absorb both. The point is not that gross sales is worthless, only that it cannot tell the two cases apart on its own: two locations with different sales, commission splits, shrink, and drive time can rank in either order once actual costs are counted, and gross sales alone gives no way to know which.

What does this calculator use instead of gross sales to judge a location?

Net profit per visit and projected monthly profit, after location commission, card processing fees, shrink/spoilage, drive time and mileage at your own target hourly rate, restock labor, and the machine's amortized monthly cost -- the same figures a DEX report or a cashless dashboard alone will not compute for you.

This calculator vs. VendSoft's route accounting software

VendSoft is vending management software: once your machines and sales data are connected, it optimizes driver routes, pulls DEX telemetry from the machines themselves, tracks inventory across warehouse, truck, and machine, and automates commission and sales-tax calculation across a whole operation. Per its own published pricing page, that is an ongoing subscription — a Basic plan at $1 per machine per month with a $19/month minimum, and a Premium plan at $2 per machine per month with a $49/month minimum, scaling with how many machines you run. (Pricing is VendSoft's own and can change — check their current page for your own numbers.)

This calculator does none of that. It has no account, connects to no machine, costs nothing this month or any month, and answers a narrower question by hand: given the numbers for one location — units sold, commission, card fees, shrink, drive time, and machine cost — what does this visit actually profit, and does a whole list of locations clear a monthly income goal?

Common questions

Should I use this calculator or sign up for VendSoft?

They fit different stages. VendSoft (vendsoft.com/pricing/) is an ongoing subscription — its published pricing lists a Basic plan at $1 per machine per month with a $19/month minimum, and a Premium plan at $2 per machine per month with a $49/month minimum — built around route optimization, DEX telemetry pulled from machines, inventory across warehouse/truck/machine, and automated commission and sales-tax calculation across a whole route. This calculator has none of that: no account, no telemetry, no ongoing cost. It exists for the question before or alongside a subscription decision — given the numbers for one location, or a list of locations, is this route actually profitable and does it clear your income goal? Many operators use a calculator like this to decide whether a location or a whole route is worth running at all, before or instead of paying an ongoing per-machine fee to manage it.

Does VendSoft do what this calculator does?

VendSoft's published features page describes machine-level and location-level profit-and-loss reporting and automated commission calculation once your machines and sales data are connected to it — so once you are a subscriber and your machines are reporting through it, it can show you similar numbers from live data. This calculator does the same category of arithmetic — commission, card fees, shrink, drive time, machine cost — from numbers you type in by hand, with no machine connection, no account, and no ongoing fee, which is the trade a smaller or newer route usually wants before committing to per-machine software.

Why would I use a free calculator instead of a 14-day trial?

A trial is the right call once you already have enough machines that route optimization and automatic DEX data pulls save real time. Before that point — sizing up a single new location, deciding whether to keep a marginal stop, or checking whether five or six locations clear a monthly income goal — this calculator answers it in the time it takes to type the numbers in, with nothing to cancel afterward and nothing uploaded anywhere.
